speechtext:
When I want
to address myself to the hon. member for South Essex (Mr. Gott), I will do so.

subtopic: WHEAT-INSPECTION, SHIPMENT AND PROTEIN CONTENT-REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
I expected a sarcastic reply
from the hon. member.

subtopic: WHEAT-INSPECTION, SHIPMENT AND PROTEIN CONTENT-REFERENCE TO COMMITTEE ON AGRICULTURE
speechtext:
The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) was
addressing himself to me, for Which I thank him.
The serious part is this, Mr. Speaker. A report goes out from this house attributing this statement to the hon. member for Kindersley, and where he is not known and where his way of reasoning is not generally understood-I know he is absolutely sincere and that he believes he is right, but his reasoning is absolutely wrong-people will say: This was said on the floor of parliament

by the hon. member for Kindersley, and everybody knows he is a truthful man, so they will think it must be so.
It seems a waste of time to attempt to refute such a ridiculous proposition as was put forward by the hon. member for Kindersley, but let me just add this: The pool in the last four years set their initial price at $1 a bushel, and the farmer pays the freight to Fort William. This year they set the price at 85 cents a bushel. Later on, just about this time of the year, the pools make a payment on account. This year they made a payment of 12 cents a bushel. The total payments on No. 1 northern in store at Fort William up to March 20, 1929, amounted to 97 cents per bushel. In other years the payment by this time would come to around $1.25, and that much at least was expected this year. The pool is not to blame for that. They set their initial price low to protect themselves and protect their farmer members. Why say that unscientific grading had anything to do with the price when the price was set before a bushel of wheat was graded? The price was based on the world's production and demand. I am not going to say any more about that.
The question of mixing was not touched on very much in the earlier part of this debate, but it has been dealt with to some extent to-day. To my mind this question of mixing is far more serious than the question of the hybrid ticket, which was dealt with yesterday. The first frost caused discontent in the country, and a tremendous economic loss; there is no question about that. The low price on the world's market, and the low payment in western Canada based on that low price, caused another great loss and a great deal of discontent. The question of mixing is probably the most serious one facing the western farmer to-day. The best organized farmers are most vehement in their condemnation of that practice, and of that I shall give evidence in a little while. Unfortunately there are two kinds of mixing: One that could be controlled by legislation and the other that probably could not. As evidence of the type of mixing that is hard to control, I propose to quote from an article published in the Regina Leader of April 22, 1928. It is headed:
Aiming at Fewer, Better Wheat Varieties, Pool backs Zoning System.
And proceeds:
Realizing the necessity of maintaining uniformity in the standard of pool wheat, the directors of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool have been actively investigating ways and means of

Grading oj Grain-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
encouraging the production of fewer and better varities in the province and have actively associated themselves with the promotion of a zoning system.
"One of the factors making for lack of uniformity," said a wheat pool official yesterday, "is the great increase in wheat varieties that has developed since the introduction of Marquis in 1903. It is true that great advances have been made in the production of wheat by cross breeding and selection by different agencies such as experimental farms and prominent seed growers, but with no restriction on the number of varieties licensed the result has been that a large number of varieties have been produced, not all of which have proved superior to the existing varieties.
"In many cases the new wheat varieites are higher yielding or have greater rust resistance but are lower in milling or baking qualities than the previous standard varieties.
I have read sufficient for my purpose. That is a situation that can be hardly dealt with by legislation, but it has been extremely expensive to the farmers of western Canada. There is, however, a type of mixing that can be controlled by legislation. In a return handed down last session in reply to a question by the hon. member for Willow Bunch (Mr. Donnelly) it is stated that in the crop year 1920-21 twelve million bushels of No. 1 northern wheat, were taken into store and eleven million bushels taken out-a little less; ten million bushels of No. 2 were taken into store and sixteen million bushels taken out; sixteen million bushels of No. 3 were taken in and nineteen million bushels taken out. Coming down to 1926-27, we find the situation worse. The practice is legal, but it is bad. In that year fourteen million bushels of No. 1 northern were put into store, and eighteen million bushels shipped out; thirty-two million bushels of No. 2 were put into store, and forty million shipped out; fourteen million bushels of No. 3 were put into store, and twenty-seven million bushels shipped out. My hon. friend from Kindersley stated, if I heard him aright, that the higher price paid by the pool was due largely to profits made on mixing. Well, if that kind of mixing can be any more profitable than the other kind I cannot understand it.
Objection has been taken to the grading system. Overseas it was complained that the grade was gradually getting lower; for two reasons; one, that the quality of wheat was gradually changing, new varieties being introduced and new areas being brought into cultivation that did not produce as high a quality of grain as the older land; the other reason for the decline in grade was the mixing. Under these circumstances it was inevitable that there should be a lower standard of grain delivered on the old country market.
There was considerable discontent, and last year apparently efforts were made to tighten up the grades. The grade delivered to the Alberta pool out of the crop of 1926, which has been quoted as a fairly high-grade crop, was as follows:
2.6 of the wheat handled was No. 1; 8.2 per cent No. 2; 17.3 per cent No. 3; 10.6 per cent No. 4; 10.9 per cent No. 2 tough; 20.5 per cent No. 3 tough; 11.1 per cent No. 4 tough.
Those were the grades that year. The balance is not divided into grades, but doubtless there was damaged grain that had to be hospitalized before it could be placed on the market. Probably last fall there was a gradual tightening up of grades- The standard grades set. by law should not have been changed. I have not heard very much direct evidence that they were changed. But there was quite an apparent difference in the commercial grades, and that again I think was for two reasons; one, that the wheat last year while it graded low-it was certainly frosted-was of unusually high quality. There had been a spendid growing season and until frost came the growing conditions had been almost perfect, and after the frost they continued almost perfect over the greater part of the west. Not since 1924, when we had a good deal of wet, cold weather, have we had such favourable conditions. Complaints were coming from the old country of the degrading of grain in previous years, and an effort was made at. tightening up the grades. That was the state of affairs when the Grain Standards Board met. As described by the Minister of Railways, it is a thoroughly representative institution. That board set the standard so high that Dr. Birchard, the chemist of the Board of Grain Commissioners, protested, and the standard set was lower than it would otherwise have been. I cannot understand why the board should be' condemned for that action of their chemist. It is unfortunate that the Grain Standards Board met so late in the season, but this point has already been dealt with by previous speakers. The reason may be better understood if I quote from the evidence given by Mr. Plumer, representing the president of the Alberta wheat pool, at the sittings of the agriculture committee on the 13th instant. I am quoting from page 18 of the report of the committee of that date.
He said:
We asked a few years ago that the setting of the standard samples be arranged at a date when our Alberta friends could be represented in them more fully than they had been up until that time, and since then we have had some better satisfaction than we had prior to that time. It is unfortunate that the samples can-
1166	COMMONS
Grading of Grain-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
not be set definitely until nearly the middle of October usually in that a large percentage of the Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan grain has moved. At that time there would be a possibility of a slight change in the standard sample.
Now, it is only natural that -there should have been a change last October if, after a series of years of low-grade commercial standards, there came a year of high-grade commercial standards. But the standard was set late in the year and apparently higher than usual. If the standard was deliberately lowered- in previous years because of weather conditions affecting the grain, it is natural that that lower standard would be reflected in lower prices in the old country according to the world market at the time. An effort was made to get it back as quickly as possible to the high standard that obtained before. I do not think the -commissioners should be very much condemned for that. It was not of their doing.
These are three of the reasons -that have caused a great deal of discontent in western Canada during the past year:	Frost-low
price-mixing of grain. The mixing gave rise to the greatest discontent. The tightening up of the grades also caused discontent.
A good deal has been said about the diversion of cars after inspection of the grain. I think that to some extent a wrong impression has been created by those who have discussed the question. There is only one legal way in which carloads of grain can be diverted. If a farmer ships his grain to an agent, whether to the pool or otherwise, and gives him authority to handle it to the best advantage for himself-the farmer-and the agent gets an offer at Winnipeg or elsewhere, and decides to sell the grain, and sends the car to the mill or the elevator people who are buying the grain, I do not see how that practice can be legally stopped. The hon. member for Kindersley said that -he was not interested in any but the pool farmers. This house cannot take that narrow, parochial view; we must be interested in the welfare of all the farmers of western Canada so far as grain growing is concerned. I do not see 'how we can legislate to compel a man to ship his grain right through to the terminal without liberty to sell it while in -transit. Ever since western Canada commenced to grow wheat there has been a degree of diversion and I expect it will continue to some extent. If, however, there has been an illegal diversion of cars by agents of milling companies or of purchasing companies, who break the seals and order -the cars diverted, without the authority or -permission of the owners or of the agents representing the 
owners of the grain, then of course it beeomes -a criminal offence and should be taken to the proper authority. It should not be laid at the door of the Minister of Trade and Commerce but should be taken to the Minister of Justice or to the police department, inasmuch as it is -a criminal action. To my mind the matter could be easily settled.
There is another ca-use of discontent-in my opinion a very minor cause-and that is the so-Oal'led hybrid -ticket. In the discussion in the -house yesterday we heard of nothing else but the hybrid ticket. But if the hybrid ticket, is the whole cause of the trouble why did we -not hear about it a year ago? That ticket was in use -by the grain trade in the handling of -the crop of 1927. In my opinion it is a wrong that should not be tolerated; I do not think it should -be used. I do not believe that the grain 'trade is living up to the spirit o-f the agreement it made with the pool. But I do -think that they are going to put up a fight-at -any rate they are likely to attempt-to prove -that they have a legal right to do what they are doing under the contract entered into by them with the pool. As I say, however, -that hybrid ticket was in use in 1927, and we heard little about it. The pools themselves were not very sure whether that agreement into which- they had entered might not bind them to some extent. As a matter of fact, -there enters into the matter a question -of considerable legal importance. The legal question involved is, I -take it, as to the time at which the ownership of the grain ceases -to lie with the grower and becomes vested in the agency to which he is sending it. Now if the pool were buying the grain, which it does n-ot do, and paying for it as soon as it was in -the elevator, there would be no question about the fact that the pool would own the grain and the farmer would not be able t-o direct shipment of it to any particular terminal. But if he were not able to ship it to any particular terminal elevator, neither would he be able to order the car in Which to ship it. If therefore he is able legally to order the car in which to ship the grain I am firmly convinced that he has a right under the law as it stands to ship to the terminal of his Choice.
The chairman of the- royal commission which investigated the subject in 1925, Mr. Justice Turgeon, has been quoted by some hon. gentlemen in this -house; and I notice that 'his opinion was quoted by a member of the house in the debate that took place three years ago. I will not take -the time now to read at any length from Mr. Justice Turgeon's statements, but this was his argument : " According to -the agreement entered

Grading oj Grain-Mr. McLean (Meljort)
into by each producer who joins the pool, the grain remains his own property until sold by the selling agency, and the producers are virtually doing their own mixing." It was in reference to mixing that he was speaking at that time, but the same principle applies. If the owner of the grain, the grower, is only sending his grain to the agency to be dealt with afterwards, then by no stretch of the imagination can it be said to be the property of the agency; it is the grower's own property until delivered. Although I have no knowledge of law, I think I am on pretty sound ground in making this statement. The amount of grain which is handled in this way is extremely small. I do not know what the percentage is in Saskatchewan, but in Alberta, according to a statement made the other day, the pool in that province handles 50 per cent of the grain; and of that 50 per cent 60 per cent is handled in their own elevators and 20 per cent of the total crop shipped through line elevators and handled under graded storage receipt, special binning, and so on. Posibly not more than 5 per cent of the total grain of that province is handled through special bins in line elevators for the pool, and I think it is no exaggeration to estimate that not more than half of the farmers whose grain goes into these special bins and is there by the line companies consigned to their own terminal elevators have entered any objection to the hybrid ticket. You would have heard more aibout it if they had. So that probably not more than 2 per cent of the growers were at all dissatisfied with it. Yet we find in this house, until this afternoon, that nearly 100 per cent of the objection to the motion now under consideration is represented as having to do with the hybrid ticket. I do not think this is the wisest way to deal with the matter.
As evidence that I am giving more than my own opinion I may say that last fall I received from many branches of the farmers' organization in Saskatchewan, which province produces more than half the grain of all western Canada, many resolutions asking for assistance in doing two things. One was to have the mixing evil eliminated in order that the high standard of Canadian wheat on the world's markets might be retained. This organization resolved that the standard for grading out of private terminals should be equal to the average of the same grade at inspection points. Technically that is difficult to secure, but that was their desire. There was another resolution dealing with the transfer of the administration of the grain act from the Department of Trade and Commerce to the Department of Agriculture.
I intend to deal with that later on. But what I want to point out at the moment is that there was no suggestion in any of these resolutions in regard to the hybrid ticket; it was not recognized as causing any particular trouble. It may be that there is a difference between the situation in Saskatchewan and that in some of the other provinces. An hon. member has referred to one difference, and it is this, that in Saskatchewan opinion against mixing is almost unanimous at the present time. The members from the province of Saskatchewan in this house, and who were in the province at that time, were invited to confer with the authorities of the Saskatchewan pool before coming here. This is coming to be an annual practice, and it is a wise one. We attended that conference and heard many matters discussed, and the so-called hybrid ticket was among them. It was also discussed the year before to some extent. At that gathering an understanding was arrived at that a written statement would be sent to the members from Saskatchewan in this house setting out the reforms which the pool was really anxious to secure and was fighting for. I hold that statement in my hand; I received it from an officer of the pool. I find that it deals first with mixing in general, the great evil which is recognized to-day by all the farmers of Saskatchewan; and regardless of what anyone says, mixing is the first evil. Damage from frost and other natural causes is an important consideration with which we cannot deal, but mixing is the paramount evil in respect to which immediate relief is asked. Another trouble is in regard to the definition of No. 3 northern wheat; a better definition is desired. The situation there is rather confused because of changes that have developed since No. 3 was first dealt with. The memorandum also covers such grades as amber, durum, No. 1 and No. 2 Canadian western, and so forth. But there is nothing at all in the memorandum about the hybrid ticket. I say therefore that it is not fair for some hon. members to make such a fuss about the grain commission in reference to this ticket.
I must hurry on because my time is getting short, and I am not so much interested in rehearsing the difficulties of the farmers in western Canada as in trying to find a remedy for those troubles; because no matter where farming is carried on, the history of agriculture throughout the world teaches us that the farmer is always just one jump ahead of disaster. In the semi-tropical zone in the southern states the citrus crop is just a little ahead of frost; a little further north the cotton crop is faced with the same diffi-
1168	COMMONS
Grading of Grain-Mr. McLean (Melfort)
culty; and the same is true of corn, wheat and other products. I presume that the farmers in the rich province of Ontario are also pursued by trouble from time to time. However, in my opinion it is better to improve conditions than to talk about them.
Now in connection with the administration of the grain act I will admit that there are inequalities; there are certain difficulties that must be overcome. Let us look for a few moments at the history of the Manitoba Grain Act and its administration for the past thirty years. That act was secured after a hard fight by the organized grain growers of western Canada; they came down here and put up a good battle and finally had the act put through. That battle stirred up and interested every farmer in western Canada, so that when the act was passed almost every farmer in the west knew exactly what its provisions were, what it meant to him and all about it. During this time the population of western Canada was small; farming was carried on in a small area, aver which the soil was very much the same and the climatic conditions very similar. The organized farmers were familiar with the 'law. In addition to that the warehouse commissioner, the administrator of the act, was located in Winnipeg, and his deputy was in the field. I refer to Mr. Snow, who has been so maligned here, in my opinion without adequate oause. However, the farmers of the west were thoroughly aware of their rights, privileges and responsibilities under that act; the deputy was in the field all the time, settling problems, meeting farmers who had grievances or who were dissatisfied or who wanted information, and in those days with a small territory involved'it was possible to keep things running smoothly.
To-day, however, conditions are different. The territory involved has increased to twenty times its former area; the yield of grain has increased ten times; there are twenty or thirty varieties of wheat now where formerly there was one, and there are thousands of farmers who are not so familiar with the act. Some may doubt that; the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) asked the Minister of Railways a few minutes ago if it were true that the farmers did not know their rights and privileges under the act. It is extremely difficult for them to do so, as is shown from the debates which take place in this house in connection with different pieces of legislation. There are times when we are in doubt as to the provisions of certain acts, so we cannot wonder that the farmer is uncertain also. The facts remains that many farmers in the west are not thoroughly familiar with their rights and privileges, and that is only natural.

I happened to listen to some of the evidence given before the royal grain commission when, it sat in Saskatchewan last fall. That commission was very helpful, not only through the information it gathered from the farmers but bv means of the information it was able to give to them. Many farmers appeared before that commission, gave their evidence on oath that they had done so and so, that they believed they could be compelled to do so and so and that they did not know they had power to demand certain other things. The chairman of the commission or one of his assistants had no difficulty in showing the farmers their position under the act, but before that many had not known of them. That is a very different situation to that which existed twenty-five or thirty years ago, when the farmers knew pretty well what was in the statute.

Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted by the request from the Deputy of the Governor General that this house should attend him in the senate chamber, I was dealing with the means which, in my opinion, should be taken to improve the handling of grain under the Canada Grain Act. A request was made last fall by the organized farmers throughout Saskatchewan for some action on this matter, and the following resolution was passed by many branches:
Whereas we believe the administration of the Canada Grain Act should be under the control of the Department of Agriculture, as it deals

. Grading o/ Grain-Mr. Coote
with the grading and the movement of the most important agricultural product in Canada, and further the Department of Agriculture, having a wide knowledge and sympathetic interest in and understanding of agricultural problems, is the logical department to administer the said act;
Therefore be it resolved we request the Dominion government to remove the administration of the Canada Grain Act from the Department of Trade and Commerce and place it under the Department of Agriculture.
When the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) was speaking this afternoon he made the statement that we would be expressing a lack of confidence in the Minister of Trade and Commerce through the passing of this resolution. It is a matter not of expressing a lack of confidence in the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but rather of expressing confidence in the Minister of Agriculture and asking that the administration of this act be placed under that department, in which department probably ninety-eight to one hundred per cent of the farmers have confidence. It would be an expression of confidence in the organization back of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell), which organization has a wide knowledge and sympathetic interest in and understanding of agricultural problems. It is agreed that the Department of Trade and Commerce is the logical department to help the farmers sell their products, but in the handling and shipping of their grain, and the solving of other problems which might arise, the farmers of western Canada need the assistance of such men as Doctor Grisdale, Mr. Newman, and Mr. Clark. Those are the men who have developed marquis, garnet and other varieties of wheat which have so greatly benefited the country. The farmers believe that such an organization back of the minister would naturally be more sympathetic than would be an organization of salesmen. They would be more effective in their own sphere, and so the request has been made that this matter be transferred to the Department of Agriculture.
I should like to see this resolution carried out to the fullest extent. I am not a member of the agriculture committee and, therefore, could not urge my views upon that committee, so I desire to move that the motion be amended by adding thereto the following words,
"and also the administration of the Canada Grain Act."

Mr. Speaker, the report which is being discussed by the house deals with a matter which is of very great importance to Canada generally, and to the grain producers of Canada particularly. Parliament also is greatly interested in this matter, and rightly so. During the years 1921 to 1927 the government has received a surplus of revenue over expenditures under *the administration of the Canada Grain Act amounting to over $2,500,000. I have been asked 'by members of this house why it is necessary to have the grain act at all: why it is necessary to have grading and inspection of grain. I think that question can be answered very readily:	It is because of the
immense volume of grain which has to be handled in a short time. It might be enlightening to members of this house to know that during one week in the year 1928, the week ending September 23, fifty-one million bushels of grain were delivered at country elevators and loading platforms in western Canada. During that same week 47,000,000 bushels of wheat alone were delivered. During one week last year over 24,000,000 bushels of grain arrived at Fort William and Port Arthur to be unloaded at the terminal elevators. Board of Grain Commissioners
Whereas the Canada Grain Act was passed for the protection of the farmers, and
Whereas the Board of Grain Commissioners was appointed to insure to the farmers the protection intented to be extended to them by the Canada Grain Act, and

Be it resolved:
(a)	That this convention demand the removal of the present grain commissioners;
(b)	That this convention request parliament to amend the Canada Grain Act to provide
(1)	A board of five commissioners, one of whom shall reside in Alberta and one in Saskatchewan.

This resolution covered the mixing of grain, and I believe the remedy they proposed for this evil is even better than the stopping of mixing by law. It has not been mentioned before, but there is a possibility of still skimming the grades even though we stop mixing by law. When samples had been taken and the wheat graded, any companj' would have an opportunity of looking it over and taking the low of that grade and designating it to certain terminals. It is quite true that this would have to be done under the jurisdiction of the Board of Grain Com-* missioners, and might not necessarily be mixed with other grades, but it would be the low of that particular grade. Other cars which were at the top of the grade could be put in other terminal elevators, and all the cars of the high of the grade could be segregated and put in another terminal elevator. The low of the grade would be setting the price of that particular grade, while the wheat which was at the top of the grade and worth more money could be offered at a premium, the same as premiums are being asked for at the present time. Those large organizations in western Canada, representative of the majority of the farmers of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, were unanimous in their agreement of this particular measure being incorporated into the Canada Grain Act. That resolution does not cast any reflection upon the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it is not a personal matter so far as I am concerned. Many members of the house have attended the meetings of the agriculture committee and they have seen the work of some of the experts of the department in connection with the grading of grain. In every case where the grading of grain was under review, technical men of the Department of Agriculture were present. Mr. Newman, who followed Doctor Saunders, was present, along with other members of the department. We all know the wonderful work which Doctor Saunders performed. He gave us marquis wheat, which was one of the greatest wheats the world had ever known at that time. We have another wheat now, the garnet wheat, and it is meeting with some favour in the old country and on the continent. In order that this wheat may be put on the market in its proper form the Department of Agriculture, along with the Department of Trade and Commerce, is shipping to Europe some 10,000 bushels of it. Who will go over with that wheat to see that it is correctly milled and put on the market in the proper shape; to see that the bakers know how to handle it, and so on? It will be the technical 
men from the Department of Agriculture When we desire information regarding the quality of wheat, the grading of wheat, milling and baking, and so on, where do we go? But when it comes to testing, the propagation of new brands of wheat, setting them out and giving them to the farmers to test, all this work comes under the Department of Agriculture, and because of that it seems to me that the only logical place for the administration of the Canada Grain Act is under the Department of Agriculture.
There is one thing more in connection with the grading of grain which I think should be mentioned in this debate. When a farmer delivers a load of grain to the elevator he receives a receipt for it, and in order that there may be uniformity in those receipts and that every elevator may
not provide a receipt of its own, the Canada Grain Act definitely lays down the form of receipt that shall be used. Moreover a penalty is attached for any violation of the form or the use of any other receipt. Section 225 of the Canada Grain Act reads:
Every person who uses any form other than those in the first schedule to this act or those authorized by the board with the approval of the governor in council shall, in case any such forms are applicable, be guilty of an offence under this act. and shall be liable to a fine or forfeiture of license.
I have under my hand the orders in council and the recommendations to the governor in council asking for two changes in these forms, and while I have no particular complaint to make in regard to the changes that were asked for, I should like the house to pay particular attention to this important fact: On May 18, 1928, a letter was addressed to the Deputy Minister of Trade and Commerce and signed by the secretary of the Board of Grain Commissioners, as follows:
Under the provisions of subsection 3 of section 170 of the Canada Grain Act, the board recommend for the approval of the governor in council, that the wo-rd "graded" be deleted from the first line of the "subject to inspector's grade and dockage" ticket, (which is designated B-l on page 82 of the Canada Grain Act) for the reason that this form of receipt was never intended to be used as a graded storage receipt but simply as a receipt that grain, which was later to be subject to the inspector's grade and dockage, had been received into the elevator.

As new supplies of tickets are about to be printed by country elevator companies, it would be appreciated if the minister would recommend this change to become effective as soon as possible.
On Friday, May 25, 1928, order in council P.C. 871 was passed, as follows:
The Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and pursuant to the provisions of subsection 3 of section 170 of chapter 86, R.S.-C. 1927 "An Act respecting Grain", is pleased to order that the word "graded" be, and it is hereby deleted from the first line of the "subject to inspector's grade and dockage" ticket, which is designated B-l on page 82 of the said act; the Board of Grain Commissioners having reported that this form of receipt was never intended to be used as a graded storage ticket but simply as a receipt that grain which was later to be subject to the inspector's grade and dockage, had been received into the elevator.
E. J. Lemaire, Clerk of the Privy Council.
The point I want to make is this: that the Board of Grain Commissioners found it necessary, in order to delete one word, to ask the governor in council to pass an order for that purpose. If that was necessary-

Is it not for the reason that the shipper must have the assurance that the quantity and quality of the contents of the car shall be sent to its designated destination? It is done for no other reason, and we have a right to expect that.
Has not the railway company the right to break its own seals at any time it sees fit?

They seal the car and give
a receipt to the shipper, and nio man has a right to break that seal until the car arrives at its destination.
The Minister of Railways this afternoon said there was some doubt whether or not the hybrid ticket, so-called, was illegal. I understood him to say that.

H my hon. friend will permit me, I did not state that as my own opinion. But I expressed my own opinion, as my hon. friend will remember I did in regard to the old ticket, that the addition of those words, or indeed of any words, is a contravention of the act.

I should like to ask what, according to the Grain Act, legalizes the use of any ticket? Is it not this? First of all, the ticket must be approved by the Board of Grain Commissioners. In the next place, it must be also approved by order in council.

Hear, hear.
If there is any doubt as to the illegality of this ticket, will the minister say that the Board of Grain Commissioners authorized it, or was it approved by order in council?

Surely my hon. friend -is not trying to quarrel with me? I refuse to dispute with him. I am in agreement with his view; not in opposition.

But why cast any doubt on the illegality of the ticket?
