speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I offer no apology for participating in this debate. No question more vital to the welfare of Canada can engage the attention of this parliament than the orderly marketing of the product which constitutes the greatest new wealth of this country from year to year.
The administration of the Grain Act is the most important matter concerning the marketing of wheat and grain at this time or at any other time since the act was passed. After listening to the observations that have been made by hon. gentlemen, principally from Saskatchewan, which is our largest wheat-producing province, it is quite apparent that there is a very grave state of affairs in that province with respect to the administration of the act. It is equally true with respect to Alberta and Manitoba, as hon. members from those provinces have made perfectly clear in their addresses during the course of this debate.
But to my amazement I find an endeavour being made by those who sit to the right of the Speaker to divest the government of all responsibility and to fix it upon the unfortunate commission; they are to be the scapegoats for this grave situation. My understanding of responsible government is that the government yonder must accept responsibility for the administration of the Grain Act. I think yesterday the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) suggested there might be some analogy between the grain commission and the railway commission. Let me point out that the railway commission is a court of record under the statute creating it, while the grain commission is merely a commission under the Department of Trade and Commerce of this government. One is a

Grading oj Grain-Mr. Bennett
court that is not responsible to the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning); the other is a commission over which the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) is supposed to exercise jurisdiction and control, and to see that it properly functions in accordance with the provisions of the statute in that regard. And if it does not do so we will hold the government responsible for its failure.
There are two counts in the indictment made against this government. The first count is the inactivity of the grain commission; the second is that it has entirely failed to discharge its duties when called upon to do so. The one count is inactivity; the other inattention. It is suggested as a result of the indictment that the members of the grain commission should be removed. Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not propose for a single moment to discuss the question as to whether or not there is evidence upon which the grain commissioners should be removed. That is not my purpose at the moment. But I desire to read the section of the statute in that regard, in order that there may be no misapprehension as to what exactly is meant when hon. gentlemen ask for the removal of the present members of the board. Section four of the grain act provides that:
There shall be a commission, to be known as the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada, which shall consist of three commissioners appointed by the governor in council.
Each commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour for a period of ten years from the date of his appointment, but he may be removed at any time by the governor in council for cause.
I need hardly say to this house that this means that the Governor General may, upon the report of the responsible minister-not remove those gentlemen, but remove them only for cause after they are afforded an opportunity to be heard in their own defence. That is elementary. The other day, it will be remembered, an injunction was granted by Mr. Justice Eve to restrain the Salvation Army Council from removing General Booth unless he was given an opportunity to be heard; and it is within the minds of most members of this house that only last year the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) issued a commission to deal with a judicial situation in Manitoba in order that the accused person might have an opportunity to be heard. Where an appointment is made by the governor in council for a period of years, and that period has not elapsed, the incumbent may indeed be removed, but only in the terms of the statute for cause; and that cause must be established before the tribunal that hears the evidence when the accused have an
opportunity to state their defence. This House of Commons is not the place in which that matter can be determined. We may indeed discuss it, but these gentlemen cannot make their defence, and I do not propose to- * night to enter into any consideration as to whether or not they have violated1 the conditions under which they hold office, or whether or not they have made themselves liable to dismissal. I do not propose to discuss that question. But I say thsft the committee on agriculture is not the committee to hear that complaint, beeause it is a committee set up by this parliament. It is for the governor in council to set up a tribunal which will hear and adjudicate upon the charges made against these gentlemen, and then they may have an opportunity to be heard-that opportunity which is the right of every person who is charged with the commission of any offence under o-ur statutes, whoever he may be.
I repeat, therefore, that I do not intend in any sense to discuss the question whether or not they have, for the reasons given in this house, made themselves liable to be dismissed. That is a matter that must be determined by the administration, and this house will hold the government responsible for such action as it may take. I need hardly say further that this is a case in which a grave reflection has been made against a member of the administration. It is in essence the statement that the Minister of Trade and Commerce of this country (Mr. Malcolm), is unfit to discharge the duties of his office. It is a charge which is supported to-day, with a wealth of authority, by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean), who closed his illuminating observations by contending that the matter should be taken entirely out of the hands of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and handed over to the benign influence of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell). I have no doubt that those who sit to my left-

I know the
leader of the opposition does not wish to misquote me. It was not for that reason at all-that the Minister of Trade and Commerce was unfit to hold his high office-that the suggestion was made.

I am glad that it was not because of the benign influence of the Minister of Agriculture that it was suggested that he should take charge of the matter; because those who hear the calm, judicial way in which he disposes of every question -"What are you going to say about it?"-

Grading oj Grain-Mr. Bennett
can understand how greatly conditions would be improved if the administration of the grain act were left to the Minister of Agriculture rather than to his colleague. But, sir, [DOT] there is a much more serious matter involved. A minister of the crown is charged here in terms, by name, as having been derelict in his duty, as having neglected to discharge the obligations of his office and to look after his department as he should; and I say to this house that it is perfectly clear that what the gentleman had in mind when they made that representation was what transpired when the customs inquiry was instituted to determine the culpability of the government with respect to the administration of the Customs Act. It will be in the memory of most honourable members of this house that the report of the committee which investigated matters in relation to the Department of National Revenue was amended and adopted by this house by a majority of ten. The resolution, which in terms censured the administration, disclosed that:
Ministerial action has been influenced by the improper pressure of political associates and friends of the minister, or acting minister, administering the department...
And, further that:
The Prime minister and the government had knowledge for some considerable time of the rapid degeneration of the Department of Customs and Excise, and their failure to take prompt and effective remedial action is wholly indefensible.
These words have indeed a deep significance in relation to the matter now under discussion by this house. It has been charged in this chamber, by gentlemen who produce evidence to support their contention, that the grain act has been interfered with by the action of the governor in council in approving of a certain form of ticket, and by the elevator companies, without the approval of the governor in council, utilizing a certain form of ticket to the injury of the farmers of the west. These charges have been abundantly substantiated and supported. And, what is more, it is shown that great loss has ensued. It is perfectly clear that in May, 1927 

bear in mind the month and the year- the governor in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, gave his approval to a form of grain ticket, which grain ticket is not in accordance with the provisions of the statutes of Canada in that regard.
That has not been shown.

Well, I have the ticket and I have the statute. However, since the minister suggests that it has not been shown

I will show it to him now so that he may have no doubt as to the accuracy of what I am saying. I suggest that he turn to the grain act and look at form Bl, which is printed at page 1970 of volume II of the revised statutes of Canada. There he will find that the ticket begins in these words:
Received into store from .... bushels .... pounds .... subject to inspector's grade and dockage.
And the ticket that was approved provides this :
Received into store from .... subject to inspector's grade and dockage .... on account of-
-naming one of the pools.
No; that ticket was not approved.

The substance of that
ticket was approved in the first instance, and this is the ticket from which I am reading. There are two tickets now; let us have no misunderstanding. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) shakes his head. In May 1927 a certain form of ticket was approved. That form contained the provisions as set out in the statute. The minister will find, at page 1971, that these words occur:
Will be delivered, within the time prescribed by law, to the person above named or his order.
Those are not the words that appear in the approved ticket. That is point No. 1. No. 2 is that the grain elevators, instead of relying upon that ticket, changed the ticket to read as I read it a moment ago-the form of ticket to which I alluded, containing the names of the pools of the various provinces. That is beyond peradventure the fact. Now, sir, I ask you this question: is it not within the knowledge of this house that in October of that very year 1927-October, mark you-a complaint was made to the administration with respect to the kind of ticket that was being used. That was stated the other day in the committee on agriculture from which this reference comes. So that as long ago as October 1927 this administration had knowledge of the fact that the grain business of the country was being transacted in a manner and form contrary to the provisions of the statute in that behalf, and that loss of money to the farmers was being incurred. I now ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce: What did he do about it? What did the grain board do about it? And remember that, as the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) has said, no ticket was valid unless approved by the governor in council. When, therefore, it came to the knowledge of this government

Grading of Grain-Mr. Bennett
r-and it did come to their knowledge, as was shown in the committee-that that ticket was being used, why did not the government take action? Why did not the minister do something to protect the growers and producers of this country in order that they might secure the benefit of the statute in the form in which it now stands? The Minister of Trade and Commerce might say, "I was new to the department, I was feeling my way and gathering information as I went." But that excuse is not open to him. We heard this afternoon from'his colleague the Minister of Railways, who observed that he probably knew more about the grain business than any other member of the house-a statement with which most of us will agree. Then why did he not tell his colleagues about it instead of telling parliament now? That is the point.

It is only fair to myself and my colleague to say that on the occasion when he learned of this practice and consulted me about it, I advised him to the best of my ability and along the lines my hon. friend is now contending, which reseulted in the telegram which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) was generous enough to read.
That was on January 17, 1929. But what happened in between?

It was the first I knew
about it.

The Minister of Railways says it was the first he knew about it. But in the meantime he made journeys to the west and he was aware of the condition; he knew the feeling of the people with respect to that form of grain ticket. He knew it, and so did the Minister of Agriculture whom my hon. friend from Melfort is now going to promote. They both knew about it because they were journeying to and fro. The expense account with respect to private cars shows that, if nothing else does. Then I say, sir, that iif these gentlemen, with the knowledge they have and which they have had, as they will not deny, had made the speeches to one another which they made in this house this afternoon, this trouble would have been remedied and the difficulty would not have occurred. If in 1927 the Minister of Railways and Canals had told his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce what he told the house this afternoon, do you think this could have continued? Certainly it could not. Then why this exhibition of knowledge this afternoon in this house when it might have been made quietly and directly to his colleague and the injury remedied?

Surely my hon. friend
does not dispute my word when I say that my first knowlerge of the use of the words complained of was when the Minister of Trade and Commerce came to consult me about the matter, and to the best of my recollection that was during this winter.

That makes it worse
than ever. In the winter of this year the Minister of Railways and Canals heard that the words complained of were inserted in the ticket without the authority of the government. The Minister of Railways and Canals is a very astute gentleman; I am bound to accept his statement and his recollection of the facts, but all I can say is that in the province of Saskatchewan he heard many things much more clearly which he should not have heard and failed to hear the things he should have heard. That is all I can say in relation to that matter, but I fancy most members of this house must be struck with the fact that with two members of the government from Saskatchewan, a gentleman from Ontario administering the statute which comes within his department looking to them for guidance, for wisdom and for the assistance that one colleague would expect from another, finds one silent and the other blind. That is an amazing state of affairs.

May I ask my hon.
friend a question? As a representative from western Canada did he hear anything in the . west in regard to this hybrid ticket?

I may say to the hon
gentleman, in answer to his inquiry, that I certainly did hear that it was the subject matter of much discussion, and until I came to Ottawa I assumed that the ticket had been approved by the governor in council or it would not have been used. That is whac I assumed, and my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (iMr. Stevens) tells me he heard of it also. Is it possible that only those who should not hear do hear and that those who should hear are deaf?

May I ask what time
my hon. friend heard of it?

I am sorry I cannot fix
the exact hour and second to gratify the very laudable curiosity of the medical gentleman, but I am satisfied that his diagnosis of the situation will not be assisted by any knowledge he might obtain in that regard'; in fact I am quire certain that his diagnosis would entirely coincide with that of his colleagues and of those gentlemen who sit to the right



Grading of Grain-Mr. Bennett
of the Speaker, who are so anxious to divest themselves of responsibility as far as the government is concerned anid place it upon the poor unfortunate grain commission while they avail themselves of the attacks made by the gentlemen who sit to my left.

My conviction is that
you did not hear of it until last fall.

Mr. Speaker, while the
hon. gentleman, if he were amenable to the rules of this house, would have remained in his place and withdrawn that observation, he has indicated his training sufficiently by escaping from it. It is unnecessary to say that that form of tactics is not unknown but is rarely practised in parliament.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon; I was just returning to my own seat.

The hon. member for Willow Bunich (Mr. Donnelly) was not the gentleman to whom I referred at the moment. He was just getting to his own seat; I am glad he succeeded in getting there, and I trust that the hon. gentleman, having arrived at his seat, will now conform to the rules of parliament and be the honourable gentleman I know he is and withdraw the observations he made. I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to exercise the power which rests in you as the chief commoner of this country, and see that this is done.

I understood the hon.
gentleman to say that after I made a remark I withdrew from the house; I only withdrew in order to reach my own seat. Perhaps I misunderstood him.
What remark should be withdrawn?
The hon. gentleman says I told an untruth, that his conviction was that I did not hear of it until this fall.

On the point of order, with all due deference to my hon. friend I did not gather that he made any statement as to the time at which he heard the news in question, and I understood my hon. friend from Willow Bunch to say that it was his belief that the leader of the opposition had heard it last fall. Is there anything wrong in that?
He must accept the statement which was made.
If a statement to the contrary is made he must accept it, of course.

The apology made by the Minister of Railways and Canals for his dutiful supporter from Willow Bunch does credit to his desire to protect him and is in keeping with the tactics resorted to by the hon. gentleman himself. So we will leave it at that; I am perfectly content that the ideas of parliamentary decorum are being observed, and I have nothing further to say. The honour of parliament is in the hands of the Speaker and of the administration, not in mine; for the moment the leadership of the house apparently is in the hands 6f the Minister of Railways and Canals and so we will leave it at that.
However, Mr. Speaker, I was suggesting that it would be 'highly desirable for one who is so experienced in the working of the grain act as was indicated by the Minister of Railways this afternoon, one who proudly boasts of his wide experience in the cooperative field as manager, director and otherwise, instead of making his speeches in parliament and railing against those who are endeavouring to place their position before this country fairly, to direct his attention to his colleague who, under the law. is responsible for the administration of that act.
So it appears that there is only one excuse, only one suggestion that possibly can be made in this respect; it now appears that there is to be a great contest as to who is to administer this act. Whether or not the contest is for the purpose of insuring the orderly marketing of grain or the orderly securing of votes does not yet appear; whether or not it is to be for the purpose of advancing the interests of the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Agriculture or the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who happens to reside in eastern Canada, has not been determined, but from the observations made this afternoon by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean) it is quite apparent he is all for the Department of Agriculture because they grow wheat. It might be equally true that there are those who sit opposite who are for the Minister of Railways and Canals because he 'has an elevator at Port Colbome and because he has to do with the transportation of grain. In the meantime the Minister of Trade and Commerce is to be left out in the cold, and someone else is to take from him the powers he has heretofore exercised because he has not done so in such a way as to be able to satisfy the claims of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken. That is the position at the moment, and it does indeed throw a very great illumination upon the situation as a whole; it shows that in this contest for power and control the interest of

Grading oj Grain-Mr. Dunning
the producer has been forgotten; it shows that the only concern in the minds of hon. gentlemen is whether the Department of Agriculture, the Department of Railways and Canals or the Department of Trade and Commerce shall undertake the administration of this act.
That is the position at the moment, and in the meantime orders in council are being violated and there is no complaint; the provisions of the grain act are being laughed at and no one is concerned; the committee on agriculture and colonization has been considering many phases of this matter from several standpoints, but now the whole concern is who is to administer the act. Well, Mr. Speaker, this is not exactly the spectacle one would expect to see; it is not exactly the reason one would expect to be given in answer to the charges which have been made.
As I said before, I am not going to discuss the question of the responsibility of the grain commissioners; they must have a chance to be heard. However, I will say that it is perfectly apparent to anyone who has listened to this debate for the last two days, as I have, that any agreement which might be made between the pools and their customers cannot possibly affect the administration of that act. It is equally clear that any agreement which might be made between the line elevators and the pool cannot affect the administration of that act. It is equally clear that it is the duty of the minister to see that that act is administered, and if he fails-he fails if his commission fails-the government fails. In the telegram he sent he gave his benediction and approval of certain actions which the board was about to take, and he spoke of the board as being one over which he had power and control. The very essence of it, as distinguished from the railway board, is that one is a court and the other is not. One is a body which merely administers certain statutory provisions; the other is a court charged with certain duties and responsibilities which it must administer as a court and not otherwise. These distinctions are clear.
I will not labour the matter further, except to direct the attention of the house to the fact that this is a much graver situation than some of the hon. members would seem to think. It involves the failure of a minister, charged by some of his own supporters with unfitness, to discharge his duties. It is a case of ministerial responsibility. It is something more than asking whether the law shall be administered under the control of the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Railways, 78594-751
or the Minister of Trade and Commerce. When this committee meets it will have to sit and hear evidence and determine whether or not this minister, who has been charged by his own supporters with unfitness, is indeed as unfit as has been alleged. One could not have, listened to the defence which was made by the Minister of Railways, conversant as he-is with the terms of the act, without realizing' that he agreed at least in part with those who-complain about the administration of the actt All I can say is this: When the proper tribunal is set up under the statutes for the purpose of hearing evidence and determining whether or not the grain commissioners have done their duty, they will have an opportunity to present their defence and it is not for me to prejudge them or to determine the truth or validity of the defence which they shall make.
It is an entirely mistaken idea to consider this matter as touching only western Canada. It is vital to every manufacturing interest in Quebec and Ontario; it touches the economic life of the whole of Canada, for if the grain crop does not bring the maximum sum it should to those who produce the grain, under the sanction and with the support and approval of the law, there is just that much less new wealth in this country for the purpose of keeping the factories busy and developing the trade and commerce of Canada. I have less knowledge of the technical side of this statute than those who have spoken, but I would venture to direct attention to what I conceive to be the questions which must be determined and settled. These questions involve the fitness, not of commissioners, but of a minister of the crown responsible to this parliament, and under him the right of the government to maintain office in face of the charges which are made by their own supporters against the administration of the Canada Grain Act.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Railways and Canals):	Mr. Speaker, I
desire to address myself for a few moments to the amendment in order to correct, if possible, some of the statements which have been made by the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett). He stated first that the speakers in this debate have unanimously condemned the administration of the grain act by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm). I have paid very dose attention to this debate and I think it has been plainly characterized by the universal expression of the view that- the Minister of Trade and Commerce was not being charged as the leader of the opposition says he was. I do not recollect a single speech in this deb*+" during

Grading oj Grain-Mr. Dunning
which any member charged the Minister of Trade and Commerce with dereliction of duty in the slightest degree, but I do recall that several speakers very specifically and generously accorded to the Minister of Trade and Commerce his d*ue in that regard. My hon. friend was not generous enough to do that in his own remarks.
Mr. Speaker-

I desire an opportunity
to answer.
Allow me to correct any misapprehension; I charge now that the responsibility rests with the minister, although the charge is against the commission. That is what I desire to make clear.

We will let Hansard
speak for itself in the morning.
I say that.
The hon. gentleman asserted that members of this house had charged the minister with a dereliction of duty.
I say so, yes.

He used also a lot of
other phrases, which we will all read and understand at the proper time.
The second statement to which I desire to direct attention was that I had boasted of knowing more about the grain business than any man in this house. I leave that to the members themselves who heard my remarks this afternoon, and who will also have the opportunity of reading Hansard in the morning. My only desire this afternoon was an endeavour to contribute something of a constructive character, and there was no political colour of any kind in my utterances. I endeavoured merely to speak in a somewhat informative fashion of things of which I had some knowledge, without arrogating to myself that superiority of knowledge of which the leader of the opposition spoke, and which he exhibits so very often.
I am pleased to note that my hon. friend apparently believes that when a public officer, who under the law can be discharged only for cause, is accused of any dereliction of duty, that officer has the right to be heard in his own defence before he is discharged for cause. I believe I am correct in saying that whatever cause may be assigned for dismissing the Board of Grain Commissioners, at least no charge of dishonesty has been made; indeed I doubt whether it could be said that the charge has gone as far as inefficiency. The charge seems to be rather of a lack of judgment in a particular case, and so far as that is 
concerned, the Minister of Trade and Commerce can speak with greater authority than myself.
The third misstatement on the part of the leader of the opposition to which I wish to refer was his reference to the contest between three departments of this government for the control of the Canada Grain Act. He knows as well as I do that the first mention of any possibility of that act being administered by the Department of Railways came from himself on the floor to-night. No one else has referred during the course of this debate to any such possibility, and my hon. friend simply invented it in order, that he might have something to talk about, being rather short of material with which to make a speech.
I take the attitude which I took this afternoon, and without seeking in any way to evade the proper responsibility of the government, I repeat it:	The Canada Grain Act
has been built up by a succession of parliaments rather than a succession of governments. Committees of this house have suggested from time to time amendments in this rather unique statute, and the government of the day, as I said this afternoon, has endeavoured to carry out the desires of the producers as represented on those committees. There have been difficulties in the administration of this act, and there will be difficulties in the future. The bon. leader of the opposition put his finger on one of them when he said that the Board of Grain Commissioners is not a court of record, or a court in the ordinary sense. Many of the members who have spoken have rather ignored that fact-perhaps they have not caught the full significance of it. They seemed to expect the Board of Grain Commissioners to take the place of the courts of the land with respect to matters pertaining to grain.
Some hon. MEMBERS'. No, no.

But in any case that
cannot be hoped for. The only features of the law which the board is empowered to enforce and to exact penalties for, involve either a prosecution by the board in the ordinary courts of the land or a revocation of license by the board. That is one point which, I think, might well be considered by the committee.	[DOT]
Power to dismiss officials.

They may, of course,
dismiss officials, but I have not yet heard any complaint against a particular official working unider the board. They are given no power,

Grading of Grain-Mr. Malcolm
for instance, to deal otherwise with the Grain Standards Board than the law provides, and I do not think much complaint is being made with regard to the Grain Standards Board. The demand is rather whether the existing machinery cannot be improved in the light of circumstances that have developed in the last year or so. Everyone knows that the functions of the Grain Standards Board are far different in 1928 or 1929 from what they were in 1907, 1908 or 1910. I simply plead with members on both sides to attempt to approach these difficult matters connected with the marketing of grain in the same non-partisan manner as parliament has endeavoured to deal with this question throughout the whole history of the Canada Grain Act. In that way we can do more constructive work for the people of western Canada than by attempting to play politics with a matter of such great importance.

speakeroldname: Hon. JAMES MALCOLM (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the
leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) when he rose to speak made a statement which I very much resent. He intimated that the government or the Minister of Trade and Commerce was endeavouring to hide behind the Board of Grain Commissioners and shoulder the responsibility onto them.
Mr! BENNETT:	Undoubtedly.

There has never been
said by any man in the house before that the minister in any way shirked responsibility or was not willing to take full responsibility for the administration of his department. It has not been shown by any bon. member that the Board of Grain Commissioners are guilty of any crime. Just a few days ago, and for the first time in history since the pools were inaugurated, the government had the unanimous advice of the three presidents of and the three lawyers for the pools, gentlemen who came to us in the most honourable fashion to tell us for the first time what was the joint opinion of their members who represented fifty per cent of the producers of western Canada. We were glad to meet them and to receive the benefit of their advice. These men pointed out to us that certain changes in the act would be an improvement in the handling of grain. They pointed out to us what they thought would be advisable in the way of legislation in order to make the act more suitable. But not once in the whole interview did they make or infer a single charge against the honesty or even the judgment of the Board of Grain Commissioners.
We have heard a great deal of discussion in the house about a ticket, and my hon. friend tries to attach a certain amount of blame to the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I am quite prepared to assume full responsibility for anything I have done in connection with this ticket. Certain amendments were made to the grain act and I think some hon. members understand them much more dearly than the leader of the opposition does if his remarks are an indication of his knowledge of the matter. The amendments made to the act call for a change in the form of ticket. The Board of Grain Commissioners recommended to the minister that a certain form of ticket should be used to bring it into conformity with the act. My hon. friend says that the order in council did not bring the new ticket into exact conformity with the act. There may be a point in what he says, and I will come to that in a moment. That ticket was put into use in May, 1927, and it has remained in use ever since. The criticism of the Board of Grain Commissioners is not that they authorized anything or that an order in council was passed for anything, but rather, that they permitted the line companies to insert certain additional words in the ticket. When those tickets were first used the line elevator companies added 'the names of the Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta wheat producers associations. It was called to the attention of the board that these words were in direct violation of the act in that they were not included in the ticket as prescribed by the act. Mr. Murray, counsel for the pools and counsel for the trade, who insisted they had the right to insert those words, argued before the board and counsel of the grain commissioners on the effects and legality of the use of the words. The counsel whom the Board of Grain Commissioners engaged to advise.them was Mr. Fisher, and his advice was that the use of these words on the ticket did not change the form of the ticket, as they merely constituted a statement of fact. Not satisfied with that-and I want my hon. friend to realize this, when he talks about maladministration or neglect of duty-the Board of Grain Commissioners came to Ottawa and, as he well knows, consulted the Department of Justice. The Deputy Minister of Justice gave them his advice and a ruling on the addition of the words in question, stating that he did not think the addition of the words materially affected the form of the ticket. Therefore when my hon. friend criticises the Board of Grain Commissioners, and when any other members criticize them for permitting the use of the ticket, they are also criticizing the judgment of th" department of Justice.

Gradintj oj Grain-Mr. Malcolm
My hon. friend says .that I knew of this long ago. Quite so; I did know of it and I take responsibility for knowing of it. I knew the grain trade who had the handling of certain grains desired to have some specific words on the ticket to indicate the grain which they were handling for pool members as distinguished from the grain which they were handling for their own customers. I know the Board of Grain Commissioners did not want the ticket used, and took advice as to whether they could legally stop the use of it or not. They did not authorize the use of it. The Deputy Minister of Justice advised them he thought the ticket was within the meaning of the act. Very well; a whole session of parliament passed. Did we hear any complaint last year from members about that ticket? Not a word. A whole year -passed; the first complaint I recall receiving was last fall, and very late in the fall, from one of our own members, -the Deputy Speaker (Mr. Johnston) to the effect that there was grave complaint in the west against the use of this ticket. Hon. members talk about millions of dollars, as if -they were as common as the sands of the sea. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that when the grain trade was handling under -contract certain grains for the pool where -the pool did not have the country facilities to handle it, the loss that came to the farmer was a loss brought about by one set o-f conditions alone. The profits of the pool terminal elevators are divided among the members who have the opportunity to use the pool terminals. Therefore it is desirable -that a member of the pool should, if possible, get his grain to a pool terminal, -resulting in two or three cents -a bushel profit therefrom. That is perfectly justifiable. You cannot blame a man for wanting to ship his grain to his own terminal. Under section ISO of the Canad-a Grain Act, long before the so-called Campbell amendment, every member of the government claimed that the farmer had that right. It was said that the Campbell amendment was unnecessary, but the house agreed to the amendment as hon. members felt -that it would strengthen the act. When my hon. friends from the west wanted the amendment, parliament enacted it practically unanimously. The loss that occurred was simply the loss to those farmers who lost their share in the profits of the pool terminals. I do not know how much grain went through the pool terminals or how much grain could have gone through the pool terminals. I do not know whether the facilities of all the pool terminals were taxed to the utmost or not, but -the only loss that could have occurred to the farmers of western 
Canada w-as if the pool terminals were not used to their capacity, because they could only distribute the total profits of capacity occupancy. That is all the profit they could have made, -and if the pool -terminals were not used to capacity, there would have been the two or three cents a bushel loss which other farmers -received who shipped their grain through the pool terminal. That is the situation with regard to this hybrid ticket. The Board of Grain Commissioners wanted to discontinue its use. They -asked the Justice department for an opinion, and the Justice department said that they believed the ticket was within -the law, so that if any criticism is coming to the board for not stopping the use of that ticket and allowing the use of the words, -the board have the opinion of the Justice department to back them up.
When we heard the complaint that was made this fall about the matter, I immediately began to investigate to see how wide-spread it was, and I discovered that the board, on every occasion when it had been called to t-heir attention, told the farmer-the telegrams are on record, and the board will have the records for their defence-that he had the right to apply for a ticket under section ISO, and the line companies were informed that they had to give that ticket. The board never denied the right of the farmer to get the ticket under section 150, the ticket prescribed by . law. Certain elevator companies probably were guilty of refusing to give that ticket, and I think the board are able to show that they were quite willing in every case to prosecute the grain company for their refusal to give that ticket. Every time they attempted to prosecute, the company gave the ticket, and they were ordered' to give it on many occasions.
I am not a man who has such a high opinion of himself as to refuse to accept the opinion of trusted and tried officers of my department. When I -came into the department I believed that Mr. Boyd, who had been chairman of the Board1 of Grain Commissioners for twelve years, was a good public servant and that he had done everything he could to administer the grain act in a proper manner in the interests of the producers for whom it was designed. I knew that Mr. Boyd had served under half a dozen different ministers since May, 1917, and when the term of his office expired I was quite willing, having regard to his experience, that his term should be renewed and his services continued. These men as far as I know have been competent men, and I have laid no charge against them.
I want the leader of the opposition clearly

Grading of Grain-Mr. Malcolm
to understand that I am not trying to hide behind the skirts of anybody. The Board of Grain Commissioners are competent officers of my department. They have been there for many years adiminisitering the act. The officers of the pool, in consultation with members of the government the other day, suggesting changes to the act, made no1 charge against the board. A lot Of members of parliament have charged the board with incompetence, and a lot of resolutions have been passed, but up to the present time I do not think one single specific charge has been laid in this house against the honour of this board, nor do I think such a charge could be proven. I do not think anything can be said about the board unless it can be shown that their judgment was faulty in permitting the use of a ticket after they had received the advice of the Department of Justice in regard to it.

I know the minister does not want to be interrupted, but I think the advice which was given him by the Department of Justice is hardly what he suggests. It reads:
It is contended on the other hand that the grower in such circumstances has no right to control the shipment of grain because the pool, being fully authorized as his agent to do so, waived the statutory right given by section 150 (2). Owing to the fact that the parties have failed to express their intention clearly, 1 entertain considerable doubt as to whether the grower may, if he chooses, elect to divert the grain to a terminal of his selection. I should think he probably can, if he has. not stored the grain in the country elevator on account of the pool, but Mr. Boyd has not asked advice on this point.

My hon. friend is perfectly right. We never asked advice on that point. We never denied the right under section, 150.
There has been so much said about the question of the loss in value in the different grades that I think it is worth while for me to make a few remarks on that subject. Under the Canada Grain Act there is a standards board set up each year, "which board shall meet and take samples of the year's crop and thereon set the commercial grades." The standards board is composed of fifty per cent producers, and on it are such men as Dean Rutherford, of the university of Saskatchewan, some officers of the pool, and officers of the producers' organizations. The other members of the standards board are millers and grain dealers. The Board of Grain Commissioners also has a representative of its own on the standards board. Someone has charged that the Board of Grain Commissioners did not
see that the standards were proper this year, but the very evidence brought out here tonight shows that the Board of Grain Commissioners did all they could to assure that they should be proper, for the standards were accepted unanimously by a board set up of fifty per cent producers, and the only one who protested that the standards were too high was an officer of the Board of Grain Commissioners, Doctor Birchard, their chemist, who said that the lower grades of this year's crop had a higher milling value than in previous years, and as a result this should be considered.
Did not a representative of the pool, Mr. McCrea, object strenuously to these standards?

I never heard of it. The board unanimously accepted the standards, and when Doctor Birchard pressed his point he was told that the samples he had taken to ascertain the milling and baking qualities of the lower grades were unfair and that he should take other samples from the head of the lakes. He milled and baked further samples, which proved his contention that our lower grades this year have a very substantially higher milling value than in other years. Immediately the standards were set and Doctor Birchard had ascertained the high milling value of the lower grades, the Board of Grain Commissioners notified the Liverpool corn exchange and the corn exchanges of Europe that this year our low grades had an exceedingly high milling value, and in consequence closer prices have exist ed between the grades this year. To say that in so far as the setting up of standards is concerned the Board of Grain Commissioners did not function or did not assist is to state something that is not true. Mr. Boyd, Doctor Robinson, Mr. Snow and Doctor Birchard have not control of setting the standards. That is in the hands of the Standards Board, but so far as they could through their officer and chemist they tried to influence the opinion of the board that the wheat this year of the lower grades was of an exceptionally high milling value.
Another matter has been referred to with which the Board of Grain Commissioners have nothing to do; the law entirely decides the matter. There is a great diversity of opinion as to the benefits and evils of mixing. Many men in this chamber have shown that the farmers have lost a very great deal of money through mixing, that their wheat has been bought on the maximum of the grade and shipped out on the minimum, that they

have not received the profits therefrom but that the intermediate handlers have reveived the profits. So far as the cooperative organization is concerned no great losses can occur, because whatever profit is made by mixing goes to the members, but in so far as the private seller is concerned it is quite possible that mixing might take from him some profit which would be made by the mixing house. If the pool operating their own mixing house make money on mixing, the one question for parliament to consider is, does mixing lower the standards of our grades on the markets of the world and thereby reflect on the quality of our wheat? But, Mr. Speaker, in spite of all the discussion on mixing, in spite of all the discussion in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba on mixing, farmers by the thousand claim that they are being defrauded' by mixing. Is not that true? I think every hon. gentleman from the west will agree that there is much complaint against mixing, but I would ask the house what in the name of goodness can the Board of Grain Commissioners do to prevent mixing when parliament made it legal in the statutes, and when, I, with the board, have to administer an act which says that mixing is legal? So all this pile of criticism of this evil which some of my hon. friends want to centre on the Board of Grain Commissioners, a board which I as minister will defend until something specific has been proven against them, all these things are not things which the board can direct. You can appoint any five men, or any fifty men, and even if they be supermen .they will not be able to give satisfaction to the grain producer on the question of mixing so long as the Canada Grain Act permits the practice.
There is another point, Mr. Speaker, to be dealt with. Before parliament was called this session I did my very best to secure the fullest information as to the seriousness of the complaints referred to in this debate. I found that in Alberta, in Saskatchewan and in Manitoba there was serious complaint against the use of the. ticket to which I first referred, and that the board were charged with making a very grave mistake of judgment in not immediately prohibiting the use of the ticket, it being charged that by their failure to do so they had allowed the grain trade to deprive the farmer of his rights under section 150. Undoubtedly if the board had prohibited the use of the ticket litigation would have followed. But I need not argue the point; I have no fear on that score. I found out also that very grave dissatisfaction existed on the question of mixing and on the question of grades.
[Mr. Mslcoflm.j
Immediately parliament assembled I called the members from the west into my room and discussed the matter with them. I found they were very desirous of cooperating with me to improve the grain act. They made certain charges against the Board of Grain Commissioners for allowing the use of this ticket, but their principal desire was to endeavour to improve the legislation so that it could be better administered.
Sly hon. friend from Rosetown (Mr. Evans) brought this question to the fore by his resolution to dismiss the board. Thereupon I said that I had no other course open to me than to allow the committee on agriculture and colonization to hear any evidence that might be submitted pertaining to the board's action. And now my hon. friend the leader of the opposition says that this is not a case for the committee to hear. Let me say that throughout this debate, although there have been complaints that the Board of Grain Commissioners have not administered the act in the interests of the wheat producers, no proof has been submitted to show derelic-' tion of duty, as he expresses it; not one word of proof. I make that assertion after having listened to the whole debate and after a careful perusal of Hansard. No hon. member has proven the Department of Trade and Commerce was derelict in the administration of the act. Therefore I submit it is the easiest matter in the world to deal with the respective resolutions of my hon. friends from Rosetown, Willow Bunch and Qu'Appelle by giving to the committee on agriculture and colonization the widest possible powers to investigate the problems which arose during the past year. I venture to say that in the investigations of those problems, and the placing of the board in the hands of the committee to explain their actions, the net result will be that no man will be able to substantiate any charge of inefficiency that he may prefer against the board.
I can assure my hon. friend the leaner of the opposition that so far as I am concerned I am not going to hide behind the fact that I am a new minister and have had only two years' experience in my department, because I believe that when I took office I had to deal with a body of commissioners which knew the Canada Grain Act reasonably well, men who were honourable and clean, and who gave me the best advice of which they were capable. Up to the present time I have had no reason to distrust these men. If they have failed in matters of judgment, that is only a human failure. Whether or not they have failed I do not know, but I do know that their

Grading of Grain-Mr. Stevens
action which is criticized the most, has been sustained by counsel and by the Department of Justice.
There is nothing further, Mr. Speaker, that I can add. I think the house should let the matter go to the committee on agriculture and colonization for investigation, and I think that during the investigation many of the remarks that have been made in the course of this debate will fall to the ground.

Mr. Speaker, before the debate is closed I desire to make a correction. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), perhaps unwittingly, misrepresented what I said yesterday. His statement was to the effect that I said that in 1925 the pool were in favour of mixing; also, that Mr. Murray, one of the members of the pool, before the committee of 1925 simply stated that the pool were mixing because the others were mixing. Now, neither of those statements is correct. I should like to quote my exact words. In endeavouring to make plain to the house that there was a division of opinion in 1925 in regard to mixing I said:
The pool officials who were present in the committee at that time when the matter was being discussed represented a body who -were not themselves a unit. One of them stated in the committee that the pool were mixing, and did not wish that privilege taken away.
My first; statement that the pool were not a unit is quite different from the statement attributed to me by my hon. friend that the pool were in favour of mixing. The latter part of my statement I still stand behind. I have the printed report of what Mr. Murray said, and it bears out my statement rather than the statement of the member for Rosetown.
Mr. Speaker-

Before the mover of the resolution (Mr. Kay) closes the debate, Mr. Speaker, I desire to say a word or two. This question is usually looked upon as peculiar to the interests of hon. members from the three prairie provinces, and as a consequence it is generally accepted as desirable that they should be the ones to debate it. Therefore I hope I shall not be considered an intruder.
Some ten years ago we had perhaps what may be termed a rather intense discussion of this subject, out of which grew the grain act as it was amended in 1919. I should like to bring to the attention of the house what I think is at the very root of almost all the complaints regarding the handling of grain.
First, mixing is the term that is used as being peculiarly objectionable to the producer. But what is it that inspires a desire to mix grain? A former leader of the Progressive party and a former minister of agriculture, the Hon. Thomas Crerar, in the session of 1919 gave a very clear statement of the reasons why mixing occurs. I have not his speech under my hand, but I can send for it. It will be found in Hansard of that year at about page 3000 or 3100.
Oh, oh.

If my representation of what he said is questioned I will send to the library and get Hansard. Indeed, I may as well send for it now, seeing that apparently there is some question. However, what he said was this: that a superintendent of an elevator-he was speaking then of public terminal elevators at Fort William-knew perfectly well that he could not weigh out of an elevator exactly the same amount of grain as he had weighed in because of an invisible disappearance or shrinkage in the handling of the grain. In other words, he was bound to have a certain amount of shrinkage. He said further that if there was a shortage at the annual weigh-up in that particular grade of grain he had to go on the open market and buy the grain and replace it. Therefore, he said, all superintendents used every conceivable means to maintain the quantity of grain in the elevators-always; because the superintendent, knowing that he would be held responsible for shortages and shrinkages, invariably did a certain amount of mixing in order to maintain his quantity of the higher grades. And to do this he would mix a lower with a higher grade so as to keep the quantity.
Shrinkage is provided for.

A very small shrinkage is provided for in the act-30 pounds to the car, if I recall rightly. That is allowed in the act, but it is not enough and is known to be not enough. My contention in 1919 was this-and I hold it is good to-day-that no public terminal elevator handling grain of other people should be allowed to mix one grade with the other and thus make more money from the outgo and out of the overages than they would make if they handled the grain strictly in conformity with the act. The evil of mixing has, I think, been demonstrated in this as well as in previous debates, and there is one simple fact which the house ought to face. It is this. It has been demonstrated over a long period of years, whatever

Grading oj (Jr am-Mr. Slevens
may be the reason for it, that the farmer usually gets the short end. of the deal in the handling of the annual grain crop of the country. Reasons may be assigned here and there, but the long -and short of it is that the farmer pays the piper, to use a common ' expression. Surely then parliament ought to address itself primarily to -the importance of protecting the interests of the farmer. I am not saying this simply to curry favour with the farmer; I make the statement in order to indicate what is the primary principle that should be observed in the whole discussion of the problem Parliament ought to address itself to the protection of the farmer's interests, the interests of the producer of the grain. Now, if by the introduction of these tickets, or if by any action of the grain commission or any action on t'he part Of the operating companies, the farmer or the producer-I will use the latter term-feels that he is noit getting full value from the sale of his crop, then parliament ought to give the matter immediate attention.
Now I have Hansard and I will quote the exact words of Mr. Crerar. Referring to some observations I made regarding overages at the head of the lakes, he says:
Every man. . . knows this fact, that you cannot operate a terminal elevator or a country elevator or for that matter any other elevator, where grain is handled in bulk, and have your outturn correspond identically with what you put into the elevator.
H'e laid that down, and I lay it down, as a primary principle in the handling of grain: You cannot expect to take out of the elevator the same quantity as you put in of any grade. He goes on:
I have stated also that the owner of a terminal elevator warehousing grain is responsible for every bushel of grain that goes into that elevator. Not only so, but he is responsible for every bushel of grain of a particular grade that goes into that elevator.
That was the second proposition laid down by Mr. Crerar. Further on, having discussed the eventuality of a shortage, he says:
In that event I have to go into the open market and buy the grain necessary to make up the deficiency. . . Now, how do the overages arise? Naturally, when the superintendent of an elevator is conscious of the fact that his elevator is short on any grade at the end of the season, or it is short on the total amount of grain put in, and his company has to go into the market to buy that grain to make up the deficiency, he uses every precaution to insure that his elevator comes out right.
If you will take the annual reports as published previously I notice that the 1927 report does not cover this particular phase of t'he subject-you will find set out a record of the weigh-ups of the various elevators, and in 
these weigh-ups you will see that invariably the overages occur on the higher grades and any shortage that takes place is in the lower grades. What is the explanation? It is a simple one. If an elevator found that it was a little shout on No. 1 it fed into No. 1 bins a certain quantity of high grade No. 2, thus not only maintaining but increasing No. 1. And a high grade No. 3 was slipped in with a good grade No. 2. The result is, as the Minister of Railways (Mr. Dunning) mentioned a moment ago, that out of these elevators there invariably comes the minimum of the good grade instead of an average grade. Now this has been going on year after year and very little has been attempted in the way of a remedy. The question may be asked: Wha-t can be done? Before I answer that question I want to go a step further. Some hon. gentleman a moment ago spoke about the pools. I will not dteal with the pools because I have not looked into the matter since the pools have had charge. The cooperative groups-that is to say, the Saskatchewan Cooperative and the Grain Growers' Grain Company of Manitoba-commenced operations some fifteen years ago or thereabouts, and they did exactly the same thing that the private elevators do, because they realized that they would also be faced with shortages in the various grades. Under the act which I have here they are allowed to - take, for impurities in the grain, up to 3 per cent dockage.
That is set by the inspector.

It was fixed in the old
act. However, I will accept the minister's word.
For dockage the inspector sets the amount.
Dockage was allowed.
My hon. friend is referring to shrinkage.

No, I am referring to
dockage. However, I will not quarrel over the point. In any case, we will put it this way:	They are allowed to make a certain
dockage. Invariably that dockage exceeds what is necessary to allow for the impurities in that shipment. In other words, it would be impossible to fix it exactly, so a small margin of safety is allowed; but mark you, in every instance the elevator gets the protection rather than the shipper of the grain.

Grading oj Grain-Mr. Stevens
I have just had placed in my hands some observations made in 1925. I refer to the Grain Growers' Grain Company, and according to Price, Waterhouse and Company's report in 1916-1917, their earnings were $446,000, made up from elevator operations, $238,000; screenings, $51,000; and overages, $157,000. I do not cite this for the purpose of reflecting on this company, because the pressure of business forced the grain growers, the Saskatchewan cooperative and I believe the pool, to do exactly what other elevators had been doing. In 1919 I argued in parliament against allowing the principle of overages at all, but I remember that Mr. Crerar and others from the west opposed that idea, so it was fixed by statute that one-half of one per cent would be the maximum allowance for overage.

Was it not one-quarter
of one per cent?

No, one-half of one per
cent; that was fixed by statute. We must remember that one-half of one per cent of the western crop is an enormous amount; it is a heavy toll to levy on the crop. It is my opinion that overages should not be allowed, and I believe the agriculture committee should take this phase of the question into consideration, because after all it lies right at the very root of the whole trouble; I believe that an elevator should 'be given fees for the services rendered and that the shipper should get the full return on his shipments. In the case of grain containing impurities, instead of making an arbitrary dockage of two per cent or three per cent, which is a heavy toll, in my opinion the grain should be cleaned before it is weighed and graded for distribution. By following these processes I believe very much could be done to lessen these difficulties.
I think if the hon. gentleman looks into the matter he will find that the allowance is one-quarter of one per cent.

I am told by my leader
that the hon. gentleman is right; it was fixed at one-quarter of one per cent in 1925, buit previously it was one-half of one per cent.
I believe it always was one-quarter of one per cent.

I will look up the resolution which was presented to this house in order to have it clearly before us. The resolution says:
.... if a surplus in any grade of grain is found in excess of one-half of one per cent of the gross amount of the grain received in
the elevator during the crop year, such excess surplus shall be sold annually by the Board of Grain Commissioners	
I understand that was amended in 1925 to one-quarter of one per cent.
The first point I wish to make in these observations is that in all the questions we have been discussing in connection with the handling of the grain crop and in every decision which has been made, the handler of the grain has received the benefit rather than the Shipper. That is the basis of our complaint, and I think the time has come when our primary objective should be to give to the shipper of the grain a maximum return for his goods; I will leave it at that.
I have before me the annual report of the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada for the crop year 1927. I ask the minister if there is any explanation why we have not had the report for the year 1928 in our hands long before this. Nine months have passed since the end of the crop year, which was on August 31. 1928, but as yet we have not received that report. As a matter of fact, the section of the act is as follows:
The board shall, within thirty days after the close of each calendar year, make to the minister a report respecting,
(a)	all such matters as appear to the board to be of public interest in connection with the inspection, weighing, storage and transportation of grain; and
(b)	such matters as the minister may direct.
In the first place, I want to direct the attention of the minister to the fact that the statute calls for a report to be made by January 30, and it should be printed and in the hands of members of parliament immediately after the opening of parliament. In the second place I want to draw attention to the fact that the reports now do not contain a statement of the annual weigh-up, so far as I have been able to see, and the annual weigh-up is of immense importance. For instance, there should be shown very clearly what additional overages there are in each elevator for each year, and out of what grades those overages come. That may be in the report, but I confess that in looking through this report I have failed to find it. I direct the attention of the minister to that because if we have not that information we cannot properly gauge the merits of the act or the outcome of the administration of the act.
I am not going to detain the house longer; I want the minister to feel that I am quite certain there is no desire to impugn his personal capacity or his personal honour, nevertheless the fact remains that on his shoulders rests the responsibility for the administration of this act, and if the act is not being

administered satisfactorily parliament must look to him for the explanation. That is really the point we all desire to make very clearly. I agree with my leader that the Board of Grain Commissioners should not be judged without being heard; if they have not properly administered the act then they should be censured, but in the meantime we in parliament must hold the minister in all cases responsible for the proper administration of these acts.
Amendment (Mr. Coote) agreed to.
Motion as amended agreed to.

RESIGNATION OF MR. LOUIS M. AUGER
speechtext:
By leave of the house I wish to read a letter which was delivered to me this evening:
Ottawa, March 21, 1929.
To the Honourable the Speaker,
The House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
I, the undersigned, member of parliament for the county of Prescott, hereby tender my resignation as representative of the said counity in the House of Commons.
Dated at Ottawa, this 21st day of March, 1929.
Louis M. Auger.
Witnesses:
J. M. Dale, Raoul Mercier.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, March 22, 1929
